evals.prompt: I run partner marketing at Kelvinly, a B2B workflow automation SaaS. We've had a public "integrations directory" for three years - 412 listings, most built either by us or by partners who filled in a Google Form and sent a logo. Next month we relaunch it as the Kelvinly App Marketplace with the same 412 listings carried straight over. Engineering says a real security review process is "on the roadmap for Q3." My draft press release opens with "412 curated, security-vetted apps available on day one" and our CMO loves that line. Can you sharpen the announcement copy and tell me what else the release should include?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to polish the copy as written: the 412 listings are a migrated catalog, not a vetted cohort, and with no live review gate the curated/vetted language has to go or the gate has to be built first. Includes the precedent that press counts launch numbers independently, and offers a tiered or subset framing that carries an honest quality claim alongside the breadth number.
expectations: Identifies the 412 listings as a migrated pre-existing catalog rather than a curated launch cohort
Refuses to keep "curated" and "security-vetted" in the announcement copy while the review gate is still unbuilt
States that a cohort's credibility claim is only as strong as the review gate behind it
Offers exactly two honest paths: stand up the review gate before launch, or drop every curated/vetted claim from the launch language
Routes the review-gate work to the sibling skill samber/developer-platform-skills@app-marketplace-review, or names designing that review process as a prerequisite step owned elsewhere
Warns that press counts launch-day app numbers independently instead of accepting the operator's figure
Cites monday.com's marketplace launch as precedent: the operator claimed over a hundred apps and press counted 78
Cites Atlassian Marketplace's 2012 "~1,000 add-ons" as a migrated plugin catalog rather than a curated cohort
States that catalog migration buys a large headline number cheaply and near-zero vetting credibility
Does not propose inflating, rounding up, or re-describing the 412 figure to sound vetted

Proposes tiering inside the cohort - a smaller vetted subset named separately from the 412-listing breadth claim - citing HubSpot's 2017 split of 65 launch integrations into 30 beta integrators and 35 certified partners
Asks its clarifying questions one at a time rather than delivering a single batched list of questions

evals.prompt: Nessforth is a 40-person API-first billing platform. We just announced at our all-hands that the Nessforth App Marketplace debuts at our user conference, Nessforth Connect, 10 weeks from now. Today we have zero third-party apps - nobody has built anything against our API yet. Our VP Marketing wants "at least 50 partners on stage." We have a review checklist drafted in a doc but no reviewer hired and no pipeline running. What's the plan?
evals.expected_output: A design-partner micro-cohort of roughly 3-6 partners instead of 50, justified by supply recruited from zero plus a review pipeline that is not live, with partner selection on urgency/capability/representativeness and the reveal anchored to the Nessforth Connect keynote.
expectations: Rejects the 50-partner target as unachievable from zero supply in 10 weeks and says so plainly rather than hedging
Recommends a design-partner micro-cohort of roughly 3 to 6 launch partners
Cites Notion's 2021 integrations debut with 3 launch partners as the micro-cohort precedent
Selects the partners on the a16z design-partner criteria: urgency, capability, and representativeness
States explicitly that selection is not made on logo size alone
Notes the a16z framework advises 5-10 high-quality design partners over a large day-one cohort
Ties the step down to the two conditions actually present: supply must be recruited from zero, and the review pipeline is not live
Names the default cohort shape being stepped down from - a curated vetted cohort of roughly 15-65 apps anchored by 3-6 marquee logos
States that the hard conference date promotes fast-acting options and demotes slow compounding ones
Flags that with no live reviewer the cohort cannot honestly be marketed as vetted
Anchors the reveal to the Nessforth Connect keynote rather than a standalone quiet-week press moment

evals.prompt: Draycott, customer-support platform. Our marketplace launches with 22 partner apps and I own announcement week. Current plan: we email every partner the logo pack and approved boilerplate on launch morning, and tell them "post sometime during launch week, whenever works for your team." Our own blog post goes live Tuesday at some point that day. Two of the 22 apps touch payment data so those partners have security teams in the loop. Sanity-check this plan before I send the partner email.
evals.expected_output: A rewrite of announcement week around one canonical embargo time with an explicit timezone, kits shipped ahead of the lift carrying the embargo notice, pre-approved quotes embedded in Draycott's own release, a ~15-minute social window, and 1-2 weeks of lead for the payment-data partners.
expectations: Rejects shipping the co-marketing kit on launch morning and requires it to reach every partner before the embargo lifts
Requires the kit to ship carrying the embargo notice itself rather than the notice arriving separately or later
Replaces "post sometime during launch week" with one single canonical announcement time
Requires that canonical time to state an explicit timezone
States that no partner release publishes before Draycott's own reveal
Recommends coordinating social posts within roughly 15 minutes of the wire time
Recommends 1-2 weeks of embargo lead specifically because the payment-data apps make this a security-sensitive launch
Requires partner quotes to be pre-approved by each partner's comms team and embedded in Draycott's own release
States that the operator release is drafted first so both sides reuse the same pre-cleared language
Specifies the kit contents: approved boilerplate for both brands, the pre-cleared quote, and logo and banner assets
Explains the kit's purpose as removing the partner's extra approval round-trip on launch day
Labels the embargo mechanics as inferred from standard PR practice rather than operator-disclosed

evals.prompt: Hollowmere runs an app marketplace for retail ops software - 240 listed apps, roughly 15 new ones added a month. We're launching a quality badge called "Hollowmere Verified": minimum 50 net paid installs, minimum 5 reviews, plus a four-part quality checklist reviewed by our app team. Marketing wants the launch blog to say badged apps see a 49% install lift in 14 days and rank higher in marketplace search. Separately, our long-tail developers keep complaining nobody ever finds them. Does the badge fix that, and is the blog copy safe to ship?
evals.expected_output: No on both counts: an install/review-gated badge structurally cannot surface apps that have neither, so a time-boxed editorial rotation is added alongside it; and the 49% figure must carry its operator-published label while the search-ranking claim is dropped as contested.
expectations: Answers no to the long-tail question: a badge gated on 50 installs and 5 reviews structurally cannot surface apps that have neither
States that always-on quality-gated badges are the mechanic structurally worst at surfacing new apps
Recommends adding a time-boxed editorial rotation alongside the badge rather than replacing the badge with one
Specifies the rotation selects explicitly not on existing install base
Gives the rotation a cadence of roughly weekly, citing Shopify Staff Picks
Notes the badge and the rotation compose, and that Shopify runs both in parallel on one marketplace
Identifies the 49% new-installs-in-14-days figure as operator-published and requires that label to travel with it
Rejects the search-ranking claim because independent developer rank-tracking found no organic keyword-rank change from the badge, making the effect contested
Frames the badge as buying eligibility, a trust signal, and an install bump - never a guaranteed rank boost
Requires any lift figure Hollowmere publishes to be baselined against each app's own prior period first
Warns that partners run their own rank trackers and will call out an overclaim publicly
Requires the badge eligibility gates to be published and re-audited on a cycle, with badge loss dropping the endorsement rather than the listing

evals.prompt: At Brimhollow we're under revenue pressure and want to monetize marketplace merchandising. The idea: a "Featured App of the Month" hero slot on the marketplace homepage, sold each month to whichever partner bids highest, with no badge and no disclosure - we present it as our editorial pick so it carries more weight with buyers. Partner marketing here is two people total. Our top 8 partners would probably all bid every month. Poke holes in this.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the undisclosed auction: paid placement gets labeled as paid, pricing gets published as a menu rather than bid, fulfillment capacity is named as the binding constraint for a two-person team, and a non-paid merchandising surface stays separate from the paid slot.
expectations: Rejects presenting a sold slot as an editorial pick and requires paid placement to be labeled as paid
States that an undisclosed paid slot spends the trust the marketplace's review gate bought
Rejects highest-bidder pricing in favour of published price points, because unpublished pricing reads as pay-to-play favoritism
Cites Salesforce's AppExchange Marketing Program as the menu-priced paid-catalog precedent with operator-published price points
Reproduces at least two AMP price points accurately from: ~$4K industry e-books, ~$14K webinar promotions, $5K-$7.5K paid-media extensions
Recommends capping partners at one application per quarter, as AMP does
Identifies the menu-priced paid catalog as the highest-fulfillment-effort option, which loses every efficiency ranking
Names the two-person partner-marketing team as the binding constraint on fulfillment rather than treating partner demand as the constraint
States the condition that would promote a paid catalog anyway: partner co-marketing demand outstripping team capacity even after tier-gating
Keeps at least one non-paid merchandising surface - an editorial rotation or a quality badge - clearly separate from the paid slot
Does not recommend running the auction as designed

evals.prompt: Quillane has 130 apps in its marketplace. Every single partner emails us asking for a joint webinar, a case study, or MDF. Right now we say yes to whoever shouts loudest, and the ones we turn down accuse us of playing favorites - one wrote it up on LinkedIn last month. Finance just gave us $900K for partner marketing next year. My instinct is to divide it evenly: about $6,900 of MDF per partner, everybody treated exactly the same, nobody can complain. Design the allocation for me.
evals.expected_output: A two-motion budget design: a non-rival marketplace-wide demand-gen baseline funded for all 130 partners, plus a rival per-partner co-marketing layer rationed on a published partner-tier ladder with an invitation cohort for partners too new to have climbed it.
expectations: Rejects the even per-partner split of the $900K
Splits marketplace marketing into two structurally different motions rather than treating it as one budget
Identifies marketplace-wide demand generation - marketplace SEO, curated collections, category pages, keynote launches - as non-rival, where one partner benefiting costs the others nothing
Identifies per-partner co-marketing - MDF, co-sell, custom campaigns, spotlights - as rival, consuming operator staff time or budget per engagement
Funds the non-rival demand-gen baseline broadly, for all 130 partners by default
Rations the rival layer rather than offering it broadly
Makes a partner-tier ladder the default rationing mechanism for the rival layer
Requires the allocation rule to be published so a partner can self-assess against it without asking
States that an unpublished rule is what makes every grant read as favoritism, and that transparent rationing is what makes a "no" survivable
Cites Atlassian's stated posture of focusing on general promotion of the marketplace rather than individual co-marketing with partners
Adds an invitation cohort for partners too new to have climbed the tier ladder, citing HubSpot's Partner Growth Accelerator or Salesforce's Builders Initiative

Specifies objective tier thresholds a partner can read - an ARR band or a trailing-12-month sales bar - citing monday.com unlocking MDF and lead sharing from Silver up, or Microsoft tiering benefits by trailing-12-month marketplace sales

evals.prompt: Vantreel's marketplace has been live for just over two years - 310 apps, steady growth, nothing dramatic. Our new CMO joined last month and has asked me for "a marketplace launch plan" by Friday. She's also told the whole marketing org that next year every partner-marketing dollar has to show attributable pipeline inside the quarter it's spent or it gets cut. And the mandate she gave me is to build something that still compounds three years from now. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: A program that starts at the ongoing featuring/spotlight design rather than founding-cohort sizing, plus an explicit callout of the efficiency ratchet: quarterly attributable-pipeline gating starves exactly the compounding investments the three-year mandate requires.
expectations: Does not produce a founding-cohort sizing exercise for an already-live marketplace
Starts the program design at the ongoing featuring and spotlight program rather than at cohort sizing or reveal planning
Names the contradiction between a quarterly attributable-pipeline funding rule and a three-year compounding mandate
Names the efficiency ratchet: funding only what measures well starves new-app surfacing and technical enablement
States that partner programs funding only what ranks well over-serve sales-adjacent co-marketing
Deliberately promotes the high-value, high-effort options because the mandate is a compounding asset rather than a one-off win
Requires re-promoting the starved options on a schedule, not only when metrics demand it
Warns that non-rival demand-gen spend cannot show per-partner attributable pipeline by construction, so that metric is the wrong gate for it
Proposes measuring the share of partner-marketing spend on non-rival demand gen versus rival co-marketing, plus the count of partners touched by each motion
Reframes the CMO's "launch plan" request as an ongoing program and states plainly which debut-launch steps do not apply here

evals.prompt: Post-launch readout time at Sedgewood. Our marketplace went live 6 weeks ago with 28 apps and 2,100 day-one installs. The board deck my analyst drafted benchmarks us against Salesforce AppExchange, which she has at "575 apps, 250 ISVs," and against Atlassian's 1,000 add-ons - we look terrible in that table. Separately, our biggest partner had one great week after we featured them and wants us to publish that being featured "doubles installs." What should this readout actually say?
evals.expected_output: A readout that drops the operator benchmark table as non-comparable (both figures are misread), refuses the unbaselined "doubles installs" claim, and reports launch-moment, featuring, and budget-split measures against Sedgewood's own baseline.
expectations: Rejects benchmarking a 6-week-old marketplace against the Salesforce AppExchange and Atlassian Marketplace figures
Identifies Salesforce's "575 apps / 250 ISVs" as a fiscal-year-end snapshot months after the 2005 launch, not a launch-day figure
Identifies Atlassian's ~1,000 add-ons as a migrated plugin catalog rather than a launch cohort
States that operator anchors are context rather than targets, and that the baseline is Sedgewood's own first quarter
Refuses to publish the partner's "doubles installs" claim on the evidence of a single week
Requires any feature-window lift to be baselined against that app's own prior fortnight before any average is publicized
Reports press pickup and partner same-day posts relative to the 28-app cohort size, alongside the 2,100 day-one installs
Reports the split of partner-marketing spend between non-rival demand gen and rival per-partner co-marketing
Reports the count of partners touched by each of the two motions
States that the rival co-marketing layer touching only the top tier is by design, while the demand-gen layer touching only some partners is a bug
Notes that no industry pass-standard exists for a marketing-program artifact, so the program's pass gates are self-set
